288.title: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza (Gittin 55b–56a)
288.hook: a wrong invitation and a public shaming; the Talmud ties Jerusalem's fall to it
288.howItsDone: The story of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza is often taught in the weeks before Tisha b'Av, the fast mourning the Temples' destruction, along with the Talmud's teaching that the Second Temple fell because of baseless hatred.

segments.voice: Yesterday four sages entered the orchard, and only Akiva came out whole. Your line was enter in peace, leave in peace. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

An invitation goes to the wrong person. It happens. A group text, the wrong contact, two people with almost the same name. Usually it's awkward for a minute and then everyone laughs. The Talmud tells of an invitation sent to the wrong man, and a host who didn't laugh. It happened, the story says, in Jerusalem, near the end of the days of the Second Temple. And the Talmud opens the story with a startling sentence: because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed.
screen: `THE WRONG CONTACT.` → `A HOST WHO DIDN'T LAUGH.` → `BECAUSE OF KAMTZA AND BAR KAMTZA.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, from tractate Gittin. A man had a friend named Kamtza and an enemy named Bar Kamtza. He threw a feast and told his servant: bring me Kamtza. The servant brought Bar Kamtza. The host found his enemy sitting at his table and said: get out. Bar Kamtza said: since I'm here, let me stay, and I'll pay for what I eat. No. I'll pay for half the feast. No. I'll pay for the whole feast. No. And the host took him by the hand and threw him out in front of everyone. And here's the line that stings: the rabbis were sitting right there, and they didn't say a word. Bar Kamtza thought: if they sat and didn't stop it, they must have been fine with it. In his humiliation he went to the Roman authorities and told them the Jews were rebelling, and set up a test that led to war. The story goes on, and it's complicated. But the Talmud's point is clear. A city fell because of a public shaming, and because the people who could have stopped it stayed silent. Historians describe many causes for Jerusalem's destruction by Rome in the year 70: politics, war, empire. The Talmud isn't writing that kind of history. It's asking a different question: what went wrong inside us? And its answer is small and uncomfortable. It began at a dinner party.
screen: `THE WRONG GUEST.` · `I'LL PAY FOR THE WHOLE FEAST.` · `THE RABBIS SAID NOTHING.` · `WHAT WENT WRONG INSIDE US?` · then, large: `SHAME DESTROYS CITIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard the table. Settle, and breathe. Think of where you'll be today: a meeting, a group chat, a family dinner. Is there someone there who's easy to embarrass, or who often gets made fun of? Picture them. Now picture two things. First, not being the one who shames them. Second, if someone else does, being the one who doesn't stay silent. One quiet sentence is enough. Hey, let's not. The bell holds the time.
Kamtza and Bar Kamtza. A wrong invitation, a guest thrown out in public, and silent onlookers. The Talmud ties Jerusalem's fall to it.
Your line: shame destroys cities. Today, don't embarrass anyone, and if someone else does, don't stay silent. Day two hundred eighty-eight.

options: stay quiet. it's not your party.

fork.reveal: in the story the rabbis stayed silent, and the Talmud counts their silence as part of what went wrong.

what it means: public shame, and silence around it, can bring down a whole community.
what a scholar hears: Gittin 55b–56a is the Talmud's moral reading of 70 CE, and Yoma 9b names baseless hatred as the cause.

289.title: Give me Yavneh (Gittin 56a–b)
289.hook: Yochanan ben Zakkai escapes the siege in a coffin and asks for a school of sages
289.howItsDone: Jewish tradition remembers Yavneh as the place where rabbinic Judaism was rebuilt after the Temple's destruction, and the phrase give me Yavneh is used for choosing to save what will endure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, and a shaming that began a war. Your line was shame destroys cities. Today, inside the city under siege. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

People who've lived through a fire often describe the same moment. You have maybe a minute. What do you grab? Not the TV. Usually it's the photos, the letters, the grandmother's ring. The small thing that carries the most. Now picture Jerusalem under Roman siege, around the year 70. Food running out. Factions fighting inside the walls. And an old teacher, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who realizes the city may not survive, and has to decide what to carry out.
screen: `ONE MINUTE: WHAT DO YOU GRAB?` → `JERUSALEM UNDER SIEGE.` → `AN OLD TEACHER DECIDES.`

segments.voice: Tractate Gittin tells it. The zealots in the city won't let anyone leave. So Yochanan ben Zakkai makes a plan. He pretends to be sick, then pretends to die. His students, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, carry him out of the city in a coffin. At the gate the guards want to stab the body to be sure. They're talked out of it: people would say they had stabbed their own rabbi. Outside the walls, Yochanan climbs out and goes to the Roman general Vespasian. He greets him as king. Vespasian says: I'm not the king. And just then a messenger arrives from Rome: the emperor has died, and you've been made emperor. Vespasian tells the old rabbi: ask me for something. And here's the choice. He doesn't ask to save Jerusalem. He asks: give me Yavneh and its sages. Yavneh was a small town near the coast. Along with it he asks for the family of Rabban Gamliel, and a doctor for a sage who'd fasted for years. Later sages argued about it. Some said he should have asked for Jerusalem itself. The Talmud gives his reasoning: he feared if he asked too much, he'd get nothing. Historians question many details of this story. But this much is clear: after the Temple fell, Yavneh became the center where the sages gathered and kept Jewish learning alive. The Temple couldn't be saved. The school could. And from the school came the Mishnah, the Talmud, and every lesson on this part of the path.
screen: `CARRIED OUT IN A COFFIN.` · `ASK ME FOR SOMETHING.` · `GIVE ME YAVNEH AND ITS SAGES.` · `THE SCHOOL OUTLASTED THE CITY.` · then, large: `GIVE ME YAVNEH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your Yavneh. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that feels big and shaky right now. A job, a plan, a situation you can't fully control. Now ask the old teacher's question. If I can't save the whole thing, what's the small thing inside it that would last? A friendship. A skill. A habit. A value. Name it. Picture protecting that one thing today. The bell holds the time.
Give me Yavneh. Offered anything by the Roman general, Yochanan ben Zakkai asked for a small town and its sages, and saved Jewish learning.
Your line: give me yavneh. Today, when something big feels shaky, protect the small thing inside it that will last. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

290.title: White face, spilled blood (Bava Metzia 58b)
290.hook: shaming someone in public is likened to shedding blood
290.carry: don't make a face go white
290.howItsDone: Jewish law treats public embarrassment, halbanat panim, as a serious wrong; teachers and parents are taught to correct privately, and the Talmud's comparison with bloodshed is widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yochanan ben Zakkai asked for a small town and its sages. Your line was give me Yavneh. Did you protect the small thing that lasts? Day two hundred ninety.

You've seen it happen, maybe in a classroom, maybe in a meeting. Someone gets called out in front of everyone. A mistake read aloud. A joke at their expense. And you watch their face. First it flushes red. Then, a second later, it drains. It goes pale. Two days ago the Talmud told us a city fell because of a public shaming. Today it goes further, and names exactly what happens in that face, with a comparison so strong it can stop you in your tracks.
screen: `CALLED OUT IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `FIRST RED, THEN PALE.` → `WHAT HAPPENS IN THAT FACE.`

segments.voice: In tractate Bava Metzia, in the chapter about hurting people with words, a teacher recites a teaching before Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: anyone who makes his fellow's face go white in public, it's as if he spilled blood. And Rav Nachman answers: you've said it well, because we've seen it. The red goes, and the white comes. The blood leaves the face. The Talmud is talking about something physical. When we're humiliated, the color drains out of us, and it looks like a small death. So the sages treat shaming as a kind of violence, not a small social slip. They go further. The same page says a person should rather throw himself into a fiery furnace than shame someone in public. And they learn it from a story in Genesis. Tamar, facing a death sentence, had proof that Judah was the father of her child. But she didn't expose him in front of everyone. She sent his things to him privately with a message: please recognize whose these are. She left him room to admit it himself. And he did. The Hebrew for the whole idea is halbanat panim, the whitening of the face. It's why Jewish ethics cares so much about how you correct someone: in private, gently, leaving them their dignity. Truth still matters. But you can tell it without draining the color from someone's face.
screen: `LIKE SPILLING BLOOD.` · `THE RED GOES, THE WHITE COMES.` · `TAMAR DIDN'T EXPOSE HIM.` · `CORRECT IN PRIVATE, GENTLY.` · then, large: `DON'T MAKE A FACE GO WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard one face. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you might need to correct or disagree with soon. A kid, a coworker, a partner, a friend. Picture the moment. Now picture doing it Tamar's way: privately, gently, leaving them room to say it themselves. What words would you use? Then, think of someone who is often embarrassed around you, and picture keeping the color in their face today. The bell holds the time.
White face. Shaming someone in public drains the blood from their face, and the Talmud likens it to shedding blood.
Your line: don't make a face go white. Today, if you need to correct someone, do it privately and gently. Day two hundred ninety.

291.title: Peace over precision (Yevamot 65b)
291.hook: the Talmud notes God softened Sarah's words to Abraham to keep peace (Genesis 18:12–13)
291.howItsDone: Jewish ethics prizes shalom bayit, peace in the home, and teaches both honesty and restraint in speech; the rules against gossip, lashon hara, discourage repeating hurtful words at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Talmud likened shaming to spilling blood. Your line was don't make a face go white. Did you correct someone gently? Day two hundred ninety-one.

Your sister says something sharp about your husband. Not cruel, just unguarded. Later, your husband asks: what did she say about me? You have a choice. You could repeat it word for word. That would be precise. Or you could pass on only the part that wasn't sharp, and leave the rest unsaid. Softer. Which one is right? The Talmud noticed that God faced this exact situation, in the book of Genesis, and made a choice we might not expect.
screen: `WHAT DID SHE SAY ABOUT ME?` → `WORD FOR WORD, OR SOFTER?` → `GOD FACED THIS TOO.`

segments.voice: In Genesis, three visitors tell Abraham that his wife Sarah, in her old age, will have a son. Sarah is listening from inside the tent, and she laughs to herself. Now that I'm worn out, will I have pleasure, "my lord being old also?" In other words: and my husband is old too. Then God speaks to Abraham. Why did Sarah laugh and say: will I really have a child, now that I'm old? Notice what changed. Sarah said, my husband is old. God reports, I'm old. God leaves out the part about Abraham. In tractate Yevamot, the school of Rabbi Yishmael points this out: great is peace, for even the Holy One changed Sarah's words for its sake. The same page teaches that a person may change a detail for the sake of peace, and one sage even says it's a mitzvah. That's a striking teaching. It isn't a license to lie whenever it's convenient; Jewish tradition takes truth very seriously, and later teachers debate exactly how far this goes. It's about a narrow kind of moment: when repeating someone's words exactly would only wound, and wouldn't help anyone. There, the Talmud says, choose peace. Leave out the sharp part. You don't have to invent anything. Often, just like in Genesis, it's enough to not repeat the thing that hurts.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS: MY LORD IS OLD.` · `GOD REPORTS: I AM OLD.` · `GREAT IS PEACE.` · `NOT A LICENSE TO LIE.` · then, large: `KEEP THE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: edit before you repeat. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone said to you recently about someone else. A complaint, a sharp comment, a bit of gossip. Picture the person it was about. Now ask: if I pass this on word for word, what does it do? Does it help anyone, or only hurt? Picture choosing what you repeat today, keeping the true and useful parts, and leaving the sharp edge behind. The bell holds the time.
Peace over precision. God left out Sarah's words about Abraham's age, and the Talmud says: great is peace.
Your line: keep the peace. Today, when you repeat what someone said, leave out the part that would only wound. Day two hundred ninety-one.

292.title: Most from my students (Taanit 7a)
292.hook: Rabbi Chanina: much from my teachers, more from my friends, most of all from my students
292.howItsDone: Jewish study often pairs learners of different levels, and teachers commonly quote Rabbi Chanina's saying to honor what they learn from their students.

segments.voice: Yesterday God left out Sarah's sharp words, for the sake of peace. Your line was keep the peace. Did you edit before you repeated something? Day two hundred ninety-two.

A grandmother gets a new phone, and her ten-year-old grandson shows her how to video call. Three minutes, and she's in. A manager asks the new intern a question just to be nice, and the answer changes the whole project. A parent explains why the sky is blue, gets asked why five times, and by the end realizes they never really understood it themselves. We tend to picture learning flowing one way, from older to younger, from expert to beginner. The Talmud has a sage who said it runs the other way too, and most of all.
screen: `THE GRANDSON TEACHES THE PHONE.` → `THE INTERN'S ANSWER.` → `LEARNING RUNS BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: In tractate Taanit, the rabbis are asking why the Torah is compared to a tree. The book of Proverbs says of wisdom: "She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her." Why a tree? One sage explains: just as a small stick can set a big log on fire, so younger students sharpen great scholars. And then the Talmud quotes Rabbi Chanina: I have learned much from my teachers, and more from my friends, and from my students more than from all of them. Three circles. Teachers give you the most at the start: the foundation, the words, the method. Friends, study partners, push you further, because they argue back as equals. But students push you most of all. Why? Because teaching exposes what you don't know. A student asks the question you'd stopped asking. They see the text with fresh eyes, without all your assumptions. And you have to explain it so clearly that you finally understand it yourself. The same passage quotes another verse: iron sharpens iron. Two blades rubbing together, each making the other sharper. That's the picture of Jewish study: not a lecture, but sparks. And Rabbi Chanina's line is a kind of humility. Even the great sage, at the top of the ladder, says his best teachers were the ones below him.
screen: `A TREE OF LIFE.` · `A SMALL STICK LIGHTS A BIG LOG.` · `TEACHERS, FRIENDS, THEN STUDENTS.` · `TEACHING SHOWS WHAT YOU DON'T KNOW.` · then, large: `MOST FROM STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your small stick. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone younger or newer than you, a child, a niece, a new coworker, a beginner in your hobby. Remember something they asked or said that surprised you, or made you see something differently. Now think of something you could ask them today. Not to test them. To learn. What do they know that you don't? Picture asking, and really listening to the answer. The bell holds the time.
Most from my students. Rabbi Chanina learned much from teachers, more from friends, and most of all from those he taught.
Your line: most from students. Today, ask someone younger or newer than you to teach you one thing, and listen. Day two hundred ninety-two.

293.title: A page a day
293.hook: since 1923 people have read one page a day, finishing the Talmud in about seven and a half years
293.howItsDone: Many Jews worldwide study the day's page of Talmud, alone, with a partner, in a morning class or through recorded lectures, and celebrate each completed cycle with a siyum.

segments.voice: Yesterday Rabbi Chanina learned most of all from his students. Your line was most from students. Did someone younger teach you something? Day two hundred ninety-three.

In January 2020, a football stadium in New Jersey filled up, and it wasn't for football. Tens of thousands of people came to celebrate finishing a book. The same book, at the same pace, read by people all over the world: in Jerusalem, in Buenos Aires, on commuter trains, on phones, in the early morning before work. They'd been reading it for seven and a half years, one page a day. Today, the last day of our taste of Talmud, we meet Daf Yomi, the daily page.
screen: `A STADIUM FULL OF READERS.` → `ONE BOOK, ALL OVER THE WORLD.` → `SEVEN AND A HALF YEARS.`

segments.voice: Daf is page; we met it on day two hundred seventy, when we found there's no page one. Yomi means daily. The idea came from Rabbi Meir Shapiro of Lublin, in Poland. In 1923, at a large gathering of Jewish leaders in Vienna, he proposed that Jews everywhere learn the same page of the Babylonian Talmud on the same day. A traveler could walk into any study house in the world and join the page. People who'd never have tackled the whole Talmud could do it one page at a time. The first cycle began that fall. The Talmud has more than twenty-seven hundred double-sided pages, so a full cycle takes about seven and a half years. When a cycle ends, there's a celebration called a siyum, a finishing. That stadium in 2020 was one of them. Think of the water on Akiva's stone. A page a day is drops. Hillel, Shammai, Honi's circle, the oven that couldn't be decided, Beruriah's reading, the orchard, Yavneh, the white face, Sarah's words, the students who teach their teachers: every story we've tasted these weeks is on those pages, somewhere in the cycle. Today, people are learning Daf Yomi in many ways: in synagogues, in podcasts, in women's study groups that have held their own siyums. The point isn't to finish fast. It's to keep going, together, with people you'll never meet, on the very same page.
screen: `DAF: PAGE. YOMI: DAILY.` · `VIENNA, 1923: THE SAME PAGE.` · `SEVEN AND A HALF YEARS.` · `DROPS ON THE STONE.` · then, large: `A PAGE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back over our taste of Talmud. Settle, and breathe. Of all the stories these weeks, which one stayed with you? Hillel in the snow? The carob tree? These and these? Let one come back. Now think of a short passage you could read today, from any text you love. A paragraph, a psalm, a page. Picture reading it slowly, the way people read the daily page, and knowing others are reading too. The bell holds the time.
Daf Yomi. The daily page: one page of Talmud a day, the whole of it in about seven and a half years, together.
Your line: a page a day. Today, read one short passage slowly, and tomorrow, read the next one. Day two hundred ninety-three.

294.title: The Baal Shem Tov
294.hook: Israel ben Eliezer, an eighteenth-century teacher in Podolia, taught that God is found in joy and simple devotion
294.howItsDone: Hasidic communities today, such as Chabad, Satmar and Breslov, follow teachings that trace back to the Baal Shem Tov, and joyful song and dance, the niggun, are central to their prayer and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed our taste of Talmud with Daf Yomi. Your line was a page a day. Did you read one short passage? Today, a new part of the path begins. Day two hundred ninety-four.

Picture a village in what's now Ukraine, about three hundred years ago. Most of the Jews there are poor. Farmers, innkeepers, peddlers, wagon drivers. Many can barely read the prayers, let alone a page of Talmud. The great scholars are far away, and sometimes what people hear is that real closeness to God belongs to the learned. Then a man starts walking from village to village with a very different message. His name was Israel ben Eliezer. People came to call him the Baal Shem Tov.
screen: `A VILLAGE, THREE HUNDRED YEARS AGO.` → `POOR, AND BARELY READING.` → `A DIFFERENT MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Baal Shem Tov means master of the good name. People often shorten it to the Besht. He lived in the 1700s, in the region called Podolia, and settled in the town of Medzhybizh. He wrote almost nothing himself. What we know comes through his students, and through a book of stories about him printed decades after his death, so it's hard to say where history stops and legend starts. His message, as his students taught it, fits in a sentence. God is everywhere, in every place and every moment, so every moment can be a way to God. Not only study and prayer, but eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. And the way in is joy. He's remembered for teaching that sadness shuts the heart, and that a person should serve God joyfully. His followers pointed to a line from the Psalms: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The movement that grew from his teaching is called Hasidism, and its followers Hasidim. Hasid is an old word, from the Hebrew chesed, loving-kindness. In the Psalms a hasid is a devoted, faithful one. Not everyone welcomed the movement at first; some leading rabbis, called Mitnagdim, opposed it strongly. Within a few generations the fiercest fighting had faded, and today both are part of Orthodox Jewish life. For the next weeks, we'll hear Hasidic stories: short, surprising, and full of joy.
screen: `MASTER OF THE GOOD NAME.` · `GOD IN EVERY MOMENT.` · `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.` · `HASID: FROM CHESED, DEVOTION.` · then, large: `SERVE WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back at this week: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, give me Yavneh, the white face, peace over precision, most from my students, a page a day. Now settle, and breathe. Think of one ordinary task you'll do today. Dishes. The commute. Folding laundry. Answering email. Picture doing it with a little joy on purpose. Humming. Noticing the warm water. Being glad your hands work. Not pretending it's thrilling, just letting gladness in. The bell holds the time.
Hasid. A devoted one, from chesed, loving-kindness. The followers of the Baal Shem Tov, who taught that God is found in joy.
Your line: serve with joy. Today, do one ordinary task gladly, as if it matters. Day two hundred ninety-four.

what a scholar hears: the Besht left almost no writings; Shivchei HaBesht, the book of his praises, was printed in 1814–15, decades after his death in 1760.

sources.work: Hasidic teachings attributed to the Baal Shem Tov
